Enmity

/EN-muh-tee/ — stress on first syllable · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Enmity is a deep, long-lasting feeling of hostility or hatred between people.

Centuries of enmity between the two nations made peace talks difficult.

Worked Example

The enmity between the rival families stretched back generations, with each side remembering old wrongs and passing down stories of betrayal to their children.

Enmity captures that deep, lasting hostility—not a single argument or moment of anger, but an ongoing state of hostility that endures over time. Simply saying "the families hated each other" would miss the weight of history and the long-standing nature of their conflict. Enmity names that deep-rooted, persistent opposition.

How Enmity Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

rivalry

rivalry: ongoing competition to beat someone, not hatred

hostility

hostility: open unfriendliness or aggressive behavior shown outwardly

rancor

rancor: bitter resentment held over past wrongs

Antonyms

friendship

friendship: warm, lasting bond of mutual trust and affection

amity

amity: peaceful, friendly relations, especially between groups or nations

How Strong Is It? — disagreement → rivalry → hostility → enmity

disagreement vs. enmity

disagreement vs. enmity: A disagreement is much weaker than enmity — it is only a clash of opinions that can be settled and forgotten by dinnertime.

rivalry vs. enmity

rivalry vs. enmity: Rivalry is stronger than a disagreement but still weaker than enmity, because rivals compete to win, not to see each other harmed.

hostility vs. enmity

hostility vs. enmity: Hostility comes close to enmity in force, but it is still weaker: hostility can flare up and fade, while enmity is hatred that has settled in deep and lasted.

Sort It Out

Now place each word on the right side of enmity.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — enem- / inimic- (Latin inimicus)

Root — enem- / inimic- (Latin inimicus): hostile, enemy (Latin)

Suffix — -ity

Suffix — -ity: state or condition of

Put it together

Put it together: Put the pieces together and you get 'the state of being enemies': the root enem- comes from Latin inimicus ('enemy, hostile') — the same word that gives us 'enemy' — and -ity turns it into the condition itself. Deep in its Latin history, inimicus was built from in- ('not') plus amicus ('friend'), so enmity is, at its heart, un-friendship: a deep, long-lasting hostility between people.

Use the root in a new word: inimical

Use the root in a new word: inimical: The desert's scorching days and freezing nights are inimical to most crops, so few farmers ever settle there.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal

Use enmity when describing a deep, long-lasting hostility between people or groups—especially when there's history behind it. For a single argument or disagreement, "conflict" or "tension" works better.
